question: We're playing best of five games to 11. In the third game, when do we switch ends?

answer.reasoning: The question describes a specific format, 'best of five games to 11', which matches the Alternative Laws of Badminton 2.0 format 'best-of-5-games-11'. Per that format's Clause 8.1.3, players change ends at the end of the third game if there is to be a fourth game — there is no mid-game change at 11 points in the third game under this format. The general Laws of Badminton 5.0 Clause 8.1.3 (change ends in the third game when a side first scores 11 points) is explicitly the clause that the alternative clause replaces ('alternative to: laws-8.1.3'), so it does not apply to this format. The ITTO 5.6.10 umpire call likewise describes the standard game, not this format.
answer.answer: In a best-of-five-games-to-11 match, under the Alternative Laws of Badminton 2.0 (format: best-of-5-games-11), you and your opponent switch ends at the end of the third game, if there is to be a fourth game: "at the end of the third game, if there is to be a fourth game". The general Laws of Badminton 5.0 rule — changing ends "in the third game when a side first scores 11 points, except in Handicap Matches (BWF Statute Section 4.1.3)" — does not apply to this format, because the best-of-5-games-11 clause is the alternative to that law.

question: My opponent shouted 'fault!' while I was playing my shot. What's the ruling?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens when the opponent shouts 'fault!' while you are playing your shot. The Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) make a deliberate distraction by shouting a fault in play (Law 13 lead-in, Law 13.4 lead-in, Law 13.4.5), and the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) clause 5.9.1.4 state specifically that a player calling 'fault' to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke is a deliberate distraction under Law 13.4.5. The consequence follows from Law 7.3 (a side wins the rally if the opposing side commits a fault and adds a point to its score) and Law 15.3 (the shuttle is not in play once a fault has occurred). All parts of the question are covered; nothing is missing.
answer.answer: Your opponent's shout is a fault against your opponent. Under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), it is a fault if, in play, a player "deliberately distracts an opponent by any action such as shouting or making gestures" (Law 13.4.5), and the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) state that "A player calling ‘fault’, etc. to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke, shall be considered a deliberate distraction (Law 13.4.5)" (clause 5.9.1.4). Because the opposing side committed a fault, you win the rally: "A side shall win a rally, if the opposing side commits a ‘fault’" and "The side winning a rally shall add a point to its score" (Law 7.3, Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2)). The rally also ends, since the shuttle is not in play once "a ‘fault’ or a ‘let’ has occurred" (Law 15.3, Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2)).

The side winning a rally shall add a point to its score. A side shall win a rally, if the opposing side commits a ‘fault’ or the shuttle ceases to be in play because it touches the surface of the court inside the opponent’s court.

question: When do we replay a rally? List every situation that counts as a let.

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) when a rally is replayed, and (2) every situation that counts as a let. Both are answered by Law 14 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26: clause 14.1 (who calls a let and why), clause 14.2 with sub-clauses 14.2.1–14.2.7 (the complete list of let situations, including the two nested under 14.2.3 via 14.2.3.1 and 14.2.3.2), and clause 14.3 (the effect of a let: play since the last service does not count and the last server serves again, i.e. the rally is replayed). No other part of the question lacks a source.
answer.answer: Under Law 14 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, a rally is replayed whenever a 'let' occurs: "When a 'let' occurs, play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again." A 'let' is called to halt play by the umpire, or by a player if there is no umpire: "'Let' shall be called by the umpire, or by a player (if there is no umpire), to halt play." The complete list of situations that count as a let is given by Law 14.2, "It shall be a 'let', if:": (1) "the server serves before the receiver is ready (Law 9.4)"; (2) "during service, the receiver and the server are both faulted"; (3) "after the service is returned, the shuttle is:" — specifically, "caught on the net and remains suspended on its top" or, "after passing over the net is caught in the net"; (4) "during play, the shuttle disintegrates and the base completely separates from the rest of the shuttle"; (5) "in the opinion of the umpire, play is disrupted or a player of the opposing side is distracted by a coach"; (6) "a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision; or"; (7) "any unforeseen or accidental situation has occurred."

question: My partner cut his hand mid-game and it's bleeding. How long can we stop, and who can come on court to help?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) how long play may stop for a bleeding injury, and (2) who may come on court to help. Both are covered by the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26: itto-5.14.2 (blood-flowing injury delay), itto-3.6.1.4 (resolve well within a few minutes), itto-5.14.1 (umpire times the delay; no undue-delay treatment on court; Referee decides who is required on court), itto-3.6.1.2 (quick relief such as a bandage; time-consuming treatment only in regular intervals), itto-3.6.1.1 (Referee and Tournament Doctor go on court when called), and itto-3.6.1.3 (maximum two persons to assist/advise, same consideration for the opposing side). Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) clause 16.3.1 covers the umpire's general power to suspend play. No part is missing, so refused is false.
answer.answer: How long you can stop: For a blood-flowing injury, per the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, "the game should be delayed until the bleeding stops, the wound is suitably dressed, or the Referee advises the Umpire otherwise" [itto-5.14.2]. The Referee "shall resolve the injury situation as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes so that play can be resumed or abandoned" [itto-3.6.1.4]. On court, "No treatment causing undue delay shall be given on court. The Umpire shall time the delay caused by the injury" [itto-5.14.1]. The Tournament Doctor "may apply a quick relief, such as a bandage on a bleeding injury, but no time-consuming treatment is allowed except in the regular intervals and then only if the Tournament Doctor estimates that the treatment can be completed (or nearly so) before the interval ends" [itto-3.6.1.2]. More generally, under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, "When necessitated by circumstances not within the control of the players, the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire may consider necessary" [laws-16.3.1]. Who can come on court: The Umpire calls the Referee onto court, and "The Referee will decide whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court" [itto-5.14.1]. "When called by the Umpire in case of injury or illness, the Referee and the Tournament Doctor shall immediately go on court" [itto-3.6.1.1]. Beyond that, "The Referee may allow a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise the injured player and help with translation. In fairness, the Referee shall allow the opposing side the same consideration" [itto-3.6.1.3].

question: Water started dripping from the roof onto our court mid-game. What happens to the match and the score?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: what happens to the match, and what happens to the score. Sources found: Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) Law 16.3.1 covers suspension of play for circumstances not within the players' control; ITTO 7.0 (5) clauses 5.11.2–5.11.5 cover suspension for playing conditions, the "Play is suspended" call, and resumption where the Umpire calls the score and "Play" — which shows the score is retained, not changed. No source says a point is awarded or the score altered by a suspension, so the score simply stands as it was.
answer.answer: Water dripping onto the court is a circumstance affecting playing conditions that is not within your or your opponent's control, so play is suspended rather than a point being given to either side. Under Law 16.3.1 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), "When necessitated by circumstances not within the control of the players, the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire may consider necessary." The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) add that "Play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire if warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions," and that if the court "is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play." When play is suspended, "the Umpire shall call: 'Play is suspended' and note 'S' on the scoring device or score-sheet, if used." The score does not change: when play resumes, "the Umpire shall note the duration of the suspension and ensure that the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then call 'Are you ready?' followed by the score and 'Play'" — so the match continues from the same score at which it was suspended, once the court is again suitable for play.

citations.quote: When necessitated by circumstances not within the control of the players, the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire may consider necessary.
Play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire if warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions.

If, during a match, a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play.
When play is suspended, the Umpire shall call: “Play is suspended” and note “S” on the scoring device or score-sheet, if used.

When play resumes after the suspension, the Umpire shall note the duration of the suspension and ensure that the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then call “Are you ready?” followed by the score and “Play”.

question: My opponent keeps flicking sweat onto the court. What can the umpire do about it?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what the umpire can do when the opponent flicks sweat onto the court. itto-5.9.1.6 directly covers a player throwing sweat or contaminating the court: the umpire reminds the player the conduct is unacceptable and applies Law 16.7 if necessary. Law 16.7.1 (with 16.7.1.1–16.7.1.3) states the three things the umpire may do for such a breach: warn the offending side, fault the offending side if previously warned, or fault the offending side for a flagrant offence. Law 16.7.2 adds that on faulting, the umpire reports the offending side to the Referee, who may disqualify. All parts of the question are covered; nothing is missing.
answer.answer: For your opponent throwing sweat onto the court, the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) (in force 2025-04-26), clause 5.9.1.6, say: "A player throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court and its immediate surroundings shall be reminded that such conduct is unacceptable, with Law 16.7 applied, if necessary". Under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) (in force 2025-04-26), Law 16.7.1, the umpire administers the breach by "issuing a warning to the offending side" (Law 16.7.1.1), by "faulting the offending side, if previously warned" (Law 16.7.1.2), or by "faulting the offending side in cases of flagrant offence or breach" (Law 16.7.1.3) — so against your opponent the umpire can warn your opponent's side, fault your opponent's side if your opponent's side was already warned, or fault your opponent's side immediately for a flagrant offence. Law 16.7.2 adds that "On faulting a side (Law 16.7.1.2 or 16.7.1.3), the umpire shall report the offending side immediately to the Referee, who shall have the power to disqualify the offending side from the match".

question: The line judge couldn't see whether the shuttle landed in. What happens to the rally?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to the rally when the line judge could not see the shuttle's landing. Sources found: itto-8.5 (line judge's unsighted signal), itto-2.5 (umpire decides when another official is unsighted; let if no decision possible, unless IRS in use), itto-5.8.3 with children 5.8.3.1–5.8.3.3 (umpire's immediate calls when a line judge is unsighted: out, in/score, or let/unsighted+IRS), and laws-14.2.6 (Law 14.2.6: a let if a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or IRS is unable to make a decision). Together these fully answer the question; nothing is missing.
answer.answer: The line judge must immediately tell the umpire by putting both hands up to cover the eyes (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 8.5: "If unsighted, inform the Umpire immediately by putting both hands up to cover the eyes."). The rally then depends on whether the umpire (or the Instant Review System) can decide: when another official is unsighted, the umpire makes the decision, and where there is no line judge or the line judge is unsighted the umpire immediately calls "Out" if the shuttle lands outside the line, or the score (or "Service over" then the score) if it lands in (itto-2.5: "When another official is unsighted, the Umpire shall make the decision."; itto-5.8.3: "Where there is no Line Judge or if a Line Judge is unsighted, the Umpire shall immediately call:"; itto-5.8.3.1: ""Out" when the shuttle lands outside the line and then call either the score or "Service over" and then the score; or"; itto-5.8.3.2: "The score or "Service over" and then the score when the shuttle lands "in"; or"). If the umpire is also unsighted, the umpire calls "Let" followed by the score — except when an IRS is in operation, when the umpire calls "Unsighted" and requests a decision from the system by raising the left hand above the head (itto-5.8.3.3: ""Let" followed by the score when the Umpire is unsighted, except when an IRS is in operation, the Umpire shall call "Unsighted" and request a decision from the system by raising the left hand above the head."). If no decision can be made, a let is called unless IRS is in use, in which case IRS decides the line call (itto-2.5: "When no decision can be made, a 'let' shall be called (Law 17.6.6), unless IRS is in use, in which case it will be used to decide on the line call (BWF Statutes, Section 4.1.8, Regulation 1.2)."). This matches Law 14.2.6 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26: "a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision; or" — i.e., it shall be a "let".

question: Can my coach get up from his chair and stand at the side of the court during the match?

answer.reasoning: The question asks whether a coach may stand at the side of the court during a match. The directly on-point clause is ITTO 5.12.2 (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26), which states coaches must be seated in designated seats and must not stand court-side during the match except during the permitted intervals (Law 16.2). Law 16.2 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) defines those permitted intervals (16.2.1: not exceeding 60 seconds when the leading score reaches 11 points; 16.2.2: not exceeding 120 seconds between games). Together these answer the question fully; no other parts need sources.
answer.answer: No. Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.12.2, your coach "must be seated in their designated seats and must not stand court-side during the match except during the permitted intervals (Law 16.2)". Those permitted intervals, under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 16.2, are "not exceeding 60 seconds during each game when the leading score reaches 11 points" (Law 16.2.1) and "not exceeding 120 seconds between the first and second game, and between the second and third game" (Law 16.2.2). So your coach may stand court-side only during those intervals, not while play is ongoing.

question: My opponent got a yellow card for swearing during the warm-up, before the umpire called 'Play'. Does it cost him a point now, and does the card go on his record after the tournament?

answer.reasoning: Part 1 (point now): itto-5.17.10 says a card given before “Play” has no effect on the score but is taken into account for later offences; laws-16.7.1.2 gives the later consequence of faulting a previously warned side, and laws-7.3 gives the point for the opposing side when a fault is committed. Part 2 (after the tournament): itto-3.7.3 requires a post-tournament report on yellow and red cards, with the exception in itto-3.7.3.1; permanence or duration of any record is none. No whole part is none, so refused is false.
answer.answer:
No point now. Under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.17.10, misconduct before the match on the Field of Play before “Play” is treated under Instructions 5.17.3, 5.17.4 or 5.17.5, and “Any card(s) given shall have no effect on the score of the match but a card(s) shall be taken into account if further offences occur during the match (Law 16.7.1.2).” So the yellow card does not cost your opponent a point at that moment. If he commits a further offence during the match, Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 16.7.1.2 says the umpire shall fault the offending side “if previously warned”; under Law 7.3, “The side winning a rally shall add a point to its score. A side shall win a rally, if the opposing side commits a ‘fault’ or the shuttle ceases to be in play because it touches the surface of the court inside the opponent’s court,” so a later fault would give your side the point.

After the tournament, the card is reported: under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 3.7.3, “The Referee shall immediately after the tournament send to BWF (or CC) a report on withdrawals, yellow and red cards, that may trigger further sanctions.” One exception applies: under Clause 3.7.3.1, “The Referee may decide not to report a card given by an Umpire, if the Referee or a Deputy has observed the situation where the card was given and decides that the card should not have been issued.” The sources do not say that this report becomes a permanent record or how long it is kept.
